questions.prompt:
Everyone yawns, yet scientists still cannot fully explain why. For years, people believed yawning brings extra oxygen to a tired body. However, experiments have not supported this idea: people who breathed extra oxygen still yawned just as often. A newer theory suggests that yawning helps cool the brain. A deep breath pulls cooler air into the head, which may help us stay alert when we feel sleepy. Another curious fact is that yawns are contagious. Merely seeing or reading about a yawn can make you want to do the same, and even dogs sometimes yawn after their owners do. Researchers think this may be connected to feeling close to others. So the next time you yawn in class, do not blame your teacher too quickly. It might be your brain asking for a little cooling.

What did the experiments show about extra oxygen?

options.text: It made people yawn much less often.
It did not reduce how often people yawned.
It cooled the brain more quickly than air.
It made people feel very sleepy at once.

Avoid difficult tasks

questions.prompt:
The moon's pull makes ocean tides rise and fall twice a day, and engineers want to use that movement to make electricity. Unlike wind or sunshine, tides are completely predictable, so power companies can plan exactly how much energy to expect. A tidal station works like an underwater windmill: moving water turns blades connected to a generator. The technology has drawbacks, though. Building in the sea is expensive, and salt water damages machinery quickly. Moreover, only coasts with strong tides are suitable. For these reasons, tidal power currently provides only a tiny share of the world's electricity. Nevertheless, supporters argue that it can work alongside solar and wind, filling the gaps when the sky is dark and the air is still.

Which connective best fills the blank? "Building in the sea is expensive. ______, only coasts with strong tides are suitable."

options.text: In contrast
Instead
Therefore
Moreover

questions.prompt:
Living near an active volcano sounds dangerous, and it is. Yet millions of people farm the slopes of volcanoes around the world. The reason lies in the soil. When a volcano erupts, it throws out ash that contains minerals such as potassium and phosphorus. Over time, rain breaks the ash down and mixes it into the ground, making the soil unusually rich. Crops such as coffee, grapes, and rice often grow well on these slopes. Farmers therefore accept the risk in return for larger harvests. Nonetheless, the risk is real. Eruptions can bury fields in a single day. For that reason, many volcanic regions now use warning systems and evacuation plans, so that farmers can enjoy the benefits while staying safe.

It receives more ash from eruptions
It is always richer than volcanic land
It cannot grow rice or grapes

questions.prompt:
When a honeybee finds a rich patch of flowers, it must tell the rest of the hive where to go. It does so with a remarkable dance. Back inside the hive, the bee moves in a figure-eight pattern and shakes its body along the middle line. The angle of this "waggle" shows the direction of the flowers compared with the sun, while its length conveys the distance. A longer waggle means the food is farther away. Other bees crowd around the dancer, touching it with their antennae to pick up the message. They then fly out to forage in the right place. Scientists once doubted that insects could communicate in such detail, but careful experiments have confirmed it. The system is especially useful when food is scarce nearby, because a single scout can guide hundreds of workers to a distant meadow within a few hours.

Mangrove trees grow where few other plants can survive: in salty water along tropical coasts. Their tangled roots rise above the mud, allowing the trees to breathe even when the tide is high. They also trap soil, which slows erosion along the shore. Underwater, the roots provide shelter for young fish and crabs, so mangroves are often called nurseries of the sea. In response, several countries have begun planting new mangroves, and early results suggest that young forests can thrive again if the water is clean enough.

What does "shield" mean in the passage?

protection

decoration

Long ago, the keeper of a lonely lighthouse had one important duty: to tend the lamp every night. At sunset, he climbed ninety-eight steps to light the flame and polish the great lens so that its beam would reach ships far out at sea. The work was lonely, and supplies arrived only once a month, so keepers learned to be careful with food and oil. Many of them kept detailed logs. One entry reads, "Wind strong, waves high, no ships seen. Lamp burning well." Today, machines operate nearly all lighthouses, and the keepers are gone. Yet some towers have been turned into museums, where visitors can climb the same steps and imagine what it was like to guard the coast during a restless night.

What does "tend" mean in "tend the lamp"?

options.text: brighten suddenly
carry away
take care of
break apart

questions.prompt:
Many students believe that staying up all night to study is a smart strategy, but research suggests otherwise. During sleep, the brain consolidates what we have learned that day, moving fresh information into long-term memory. People who are deprived of sleep often struggle to recall facts, even if they studied for hours. In one experiment, two groups memorized the same list of words. The group that slept for eight hours afterward remembered about twenty percent more than the group that stayed awake. Sleep is also vital for mood and attention. Tired people tend to react more strongly to small problems, and their concentration drops in the afternoon. Doctors therefore recommend keeping a regular schedule, avoiding screens before bed, and studying in short sessions rather than one long marathon. A good night's rest, they say, is not a break from learning; it is part of it.

What does "consolidates" mean in the passage?

strengthens and organizes
forgets completely
repeats aloud

questions.prompt:
Every winter, city workers spread salt on roads and sidewalks. The reason is simple: salt lowers the temperature at which water freezes, so ice melts even when the air is below zero. As a result, accidents drop and buses keep running. However, this solution has a hidden cost. When the snow melts, the salty water flows into the soil and nearby streams. Young trees along busy roads often turn brown in spring because their roots cannot take in enough water from salty ground. Salt also speeds up rust on cars and bridges, which means higher repair bills. Some towns therefore mix the salt with sand or sprinkle it only on the most dangerous hills and corners. Safety clearly matters most, but careful use lets towns protect people without damaging the places they live in.

questions.prompt:
For decades, libraries charged a small fine for every day a book was late. The idea seemed fair: if borrowers had to pay, they would return books on time. Yet several libraries that stopped charging fines have reported a surprising result. Overdue books came back at almost the same rate as before. What changed was who walked through the door. Families who once avoided the library because they owed money returned, and the number of active cardholders grew. In other words, the fines had not really made people responsible; they had mostly kept the poorest readers away. Of course, there are worries. Some librarians fear that books will stay out longer and that fewer copies will be available for others. Because of this, many libraries now send friendly reminders and set a limit on how many items a person can borrow at once. Their experience suggests that kindness can work as well as punishment, and sometimes better.

Books were returned at nearly the same rate as before.
Most borrowers kept their books for a whole year or more.

Automatic systems could do the main tasks without people.
Ships stopped traveling along the rocky coasts for good.

questions.prompt:
Many people joke that weather forecasts are always wrong, but the truth is more interesting. A forecast of rain tomorrow is right most of the time, because computers can track large systems of clouds and wind across the whole planet. The further into the future we look, however, the less reliable the prediction becomes. Small errors in today's measurements grow bigger each day, so a seven-day forecast is much less certain than a one-day forecast. This is why forecasters often say 'a 30 percent chance of rain' instead of 'it will rain'. The number does not mean that it will rain on thirty percent of the city; it means that, on days with similar conditions, rain fell about three times out of ten. People who ignore this advice may feel cheated when a sunny day follows a warning. In fact, the forecast may have been correct. A fair judgment requires many days, not one.

options.text: Forecasters stop working after the first day of the week.
Small measurement errors grow larger as time passes.
Wind systems disappear after twenty-four hours have passed.
Computers cannot track clouds for more than a single day.

questions.prompt:
Every year, dictionary editors announce a list of new words, and every year some readers protest. They believe a dictionary should protect the language, not follow its changes. The editors disagree. A dictionary, they say, is like a map: it does not decide where the roads go, it records where people actually walk. A word is added only after careful observation. Editors collect examples from books, news articles and speech, and they wait to see whether the word appears for several years in many different places. A funny expression used by a few friends for one summer will not qualify. For example, 'selfie' entered dictionaries only after it had become common in several countries. Some words also leave the book when nobody uses them, although this happens slowly. Critics may still complain, but the process is a record of the community's habits rather than a judgment about good or bad English.

When do dictionary editors add a word?

As soon as a famous speaker says it once.
Whenever a group of friends invents it.
Only when readers vote for it each summer.

questions.prompt:
Every year, dictionary editors announce a list of new words, and every year some readers protest. They believe a dictionary should protect the language, not follow its changes. The editors disagree. A dictionary, they say, is like a map: it does not decide where the roads go, it records where people actually walk. A word is added only after careful observation. Editors collect examples from books, news articles and speech, and they wait to see whether the word appears for several years in many different places. A funny expression used by a few friends for one summer will not qualify. For example, 'selfie' entered dictionaries only after it had become common in several countries. Some words also leave the book when nobody uses them, although this happens slowly. Critics may still complain, but the process is a record of the community's habits rather than a judgment about good or bad English.

options.text: To explain how to find words in alphabetical order.
To suggest that dictionaries are hard to carry.
To show that it records what people do rather than controlling it.
To prove that old words are more useful than new ones.

Neighbors leave extra vegetables, bread or cooked meals inside, and anyone who needs food can take what they like, with no questions asked. Within weeks, the fridge was emptied every evening. Some residents worry that the fridge might attract mice or spread illness, so volunteers wipe it clean daily and check the dates on every item. Others fear that people will take more than they need. In practice, this rarely happens; most users take one meal and leave a little something in return. The fridge has not solved hunger in the town, yet it has made neighbors talk to each other, and that, the owner says, is an unexpected gift.

options.text: She saw that a lot of good food was being thrown away.
Her neighbors were all unable to cook at home.
A food bank nearby had asked her to open the fridge.
The town council had paid her to run a bakery.

Everyone began to wash their hands with a cleaning liquid.
Midwives were no longer allowed to help with births.
The hospital moved into a cleaner new building.

On free days, the lines stretch around the corner, and the galleries are noisier than usual. Some regular visitors prefer the quiet of an ordinary weekday and avoid the crowds. the fact that over half of first-time visitors returned
the lines of visitors around the corner

questions.prompt:
Mina had planned to bake a birthday cake for her grandmother, and she had followed the recipe carefully. But when she opened the oven, she found a flat, heavy disk. She was disappointed, and for a moment she wanted to buy a cake from the bakery. Instead, she checked the recipe again and noticed that she had forgotten the baking powder. That small ingredient, she realized, is what makes a cake rise. Because the shops were still open, she hurried out, bought a packet and started over. This time, she measured everything twice. The second cake was light and golden, though it was a little late. Her grandmother laughed when she heard the story and said that she would keep a slice of the flat cake too. 'A mistake that you understand,' she said, 'is worth more than a lucky success.' Mina agreed, and she wrote the lesson on the recipe card.

Why did Mina's first cake come out flat?

options.text: She measured the flour twice.
She had forgotten the baking powder.
The oven was set at a low temperature.
She opened the oven too early.

Customer: Could I have a refund instead? I don't think I'll find anything else I like.
Clerk: Refunds need the receipt, but credit lasts a year, so you won't need to hurry.
Customer: In that case, store credit is fine. Thank you for your patience.

options.text: It tells the clerk how much store credit is left.
It proves that the item was bought in that shop.
It lets the shop search the customer's card.
It shows that the sleeves are too long.

It promises something that the council cannot change.

Haru: That seems reasonable. I'll message him tonight.

Why does Haru hesitate about leaving the science fair early?

options.text: He dislikes the judges at the fair.
The match field is too close to the school.
His project has not been finished.
He might miss the awards ceremony.

questions.prompt:
Ayla: Excuse me, are you the librarian? There's a group talking loudly on the third floor.
Librarian: Thank you for telling me. That floor is marked as a quiet zone.
Ayla: I know, but they've been there for an hour.
Librarian: Have you asked them to lower their voices?
Ayla: Not yet. I thought they might be annoyed.
Librarian: People often don't realize how far their voices travel, so a polite request usually works.
Ayla: What if they refuse?
Librarian: Then come back and I'll speak to them. But I'd try first. Complaining to staff can feel less friendly.
Ayla: You're right. Besides, if they know me, they might be quieter next time.
Librarian: Exactly. And if you need silence urgently, the study rooms on the second floor are free this afternoon.
Ayla: Thanks. I'll go and talk to them first.

Why does the librarian suggest asking the group politely first?

options.text: The library has no rule about noise on any floor.
Staff are not allowed to speak to the visitors.
People often do not realize how far their voices travel.
The group is already planning to leave the library soon.

questions.prompt:
Nurse: Your note says your eyes hurt in the afternoon. How many hours do you spend on a screen?
Student: Maybe seven or eight, because I study online and then play games.
Nurse: That's a lot. When you stare at a screen, you blink less often, so your eyes become dry.
Student: Is that why they feel itchy?
Nurse: Likely, yes. Dry eyes also get tired more quickly.
Student: What can I do? I can't stop studying.
Nurse: You don't need to. Try the twenty-twenty-twenty rule: every twenty minutes, look at something twenty feet away for twenty seconds.
Student: That sounds easy. Will it really help?
Nurse: It gives the eye muscles a rest, so the effect is usually noticeable within a week.
Student: What if the pain continues?
Nurse: Then see an eye doctor, since glasses might be needed.
Student: I'll try the rule first. Thank you.

According to the nurse, why do the student's eyes feel dry?

options.text: Staring at a screen makes people blink less often.
Studying online lowers the temperature of the room.
Playing games makes the eyes water too much.
The student has not been wearing glasses at school.

Student: Maybe seven or eight, because I study online and then play games.
Nurse: That's a lot. When you stare at a screen, you blink less often, so your eyes become dry.
Student: Is that why they feel itchy?
Nurse: Likely, yes. Dry eyes also get tired more quickly.
Student: What can I do? I can't stop studying.
Nurse: You don't need to. Try the twenty-twenty-twenty rule: every twenty minutes, look at something twenty feet away for twenty seconds.
Student: That sounds easy. Will it really help?
Nurse: It gives the eye muscles a rest, so the effect is usually noticeable within a week.
Student: What if the pain continues?
Nurse: Then see an eye doctor, since glasses might be needed.
Student: I'll try the rule first. Thank you.

Why does the nurse mention glasses at the end?

options.text: To tell the student to stop wearing glasses.
To explain a possible reason for continuing pain.
To warn that screens can damage a pair of glasses.
To suggest that games always cause bad eyesight.

questions.prompt:

Omar: How many reviews are there?
Nari: Only twelve, but they're all very positive.
Omar: That might be a warning sign. A small number of reviews can be unreliable.
Nari: Why? Every reviewer gave five stars.
Omar: Exactly. Real opinions usually vary, so perfect scores can mean that the seller wrote some of them.
Nari: I hadn't thought of that. How can I tell?
Omar: Look for detailed reviews with pros and cons, and check whether the dates are all the same.
Nari: Several were posted on the same day. And they all use the word 'amazing'.
Omar: That does look suspicious. Compare them with a model that has hundreds of reviews, even if the score is 4.4.
Nari: A lower score from more people might be more honest, then.
Omar: Right. You'd get a truer picture.

Why does Omar think perfect scores can be a warning sign?

options.text: Customers prefer to buy products without any stars.
Sellers are not allowed to read the reviews of their goods.
Headphones rarely receive any reviews from buyers.
Real opinions usually vary from person to person.

Lena: That's a clever way to save money. Is it difficult?
Mr. Ortiz: Not at all. You turn the pile once a week so air can get in. Without air, it rots slowly and does smell bad.
Lena: Hmm. I live in an apartment, though. I only have a balcony.
Mr. Ortiz: You can still try. A small closed container works if you keep it dry.
Lena: Then I might start with a small box.

According to Mr. Ortiz, why does his compost not smell bad?

options.text: He adds only plant waste and turns the pile for air.
He keeps the bin far away from the flower beds.
He covers it tightly so that no air can enter.
He mixes it with fertilizer once each month.

Librarian: Let me scan it. Hmm. Forty-two days overdue. That comes to twenty-one dollars.
Student: Twenty-one dollars. For one novel. I could have bought it new.
Librarian: You could have. But then you would have missed the pleasure of paying for it three times.
Student: Is that supposed to be a joke?
Librarian: A small one. Here is the thing: the library has a Forgiveness Week this month. Anyone returning a long-overdue book can read to the children on Saturday morning instead of paying.
Student: Read aloud? To children? I would be terrible.
Librarian: Everybody says that. Then twelve small faces look up at them, and suddenly they are brilliant.
Student: Hmm. What time on Saturday?
Librarian: Ten. Shall I put your name down?
Student: Yes. But if the children throw books at me, I am blaming you.
Librarian: Noted.

Which description best fits the librarian's manner?

options.text: Dry humor with real kindness
Nervous and apologetic
Cold and strict
Angry and mocking

questions.prompt:
At four in the morning the bakery on Alder Lane is the warmest room in the neighborhood. Marisol rolls her sleeves above her elbows and slides the first trays into the ovens, humming a tune she can never name. Outside, the street lamps still glow orange, and nobody has yet walked past the window. Inside, the air is thick with butter and yeast, and the radio murmurs a weather report to no one. She does not mind the hour. Years ago she dreaded alarm clocks; now she thinks of these dark, unhurried hours as her own private secret. By six, the first customers will arrive, stamping their boots and complaining about the cold, and the quiet will break into cheerful noise. But for now there is only the soft thud of dough on the table, the slow rising of golden loaves, and a contentment so complete that she would not trade it for any office or any view.

Which phrase best describes the atmosphere in the bakery before six o'clock?

options.text: Snug and peaceful
Tense and rushed
Cold and lonely
Dull and bitter

Thank you, thank you, please sit down; my knees are shaking harder than yours. When our coach told us in September that we would finish last in the league, I remember thinking that was generous. We had one working ball, a field that flooded whenever it drizzled, and a goalkeeper who was afraid of the ball. (That is you, Tomas, and I say it with love.) Yet here we are, holding this trophy, which, I notice, is lighter than I expected and heavier than I deserve. I should confess that I did not score the winning goal. I did not even touch the ball in the final. I stood at midfield shouting advice that nobody followed. This victory belongs to the seventeen people who ran when they were tired, laughed when they lost, and turned up on rainy Tuesdays. So tonight, please do not clap for me. Clap for the flooded field, for the single ball, and for Tomas, who, I am told, saved four penalties last week. I am still in shock.

options.text: Boastful and demanding
Humorous and modest
Bitter and complaining
Solemn and formal

The attic smelled of cedar and forgotten summers. She turned the instrument over once more, then closed the case gently, as if the thing might wake. She still needed the blanket. She had counted the ceiling tiles twice. She had read the poster about hand-washing three times. Across from her, a vending machine hummed to itself, and she had bought nothing from it because her hands refused to stop trembling. Her brother had gone in for the operation at eight; it was now almost noon. Each time a door opened, her heart lurched, and each time it was only a cleaner, a visitor, a nurse hurrying elsewhere. Finally the door of 308 swung wide, and a surgeon in a pale blue cap stepped out, pulling off her gloves. She looked tired; then she smiled. "He is awake," she said, "and he is already asking for toast." Rina laughed, and the laugh turned into something else halfway through, and for a long moment she could not speak at all.

Which description best fits the mood of the passage?

options.text: Excitement that turns into regret
Calm that turns into fear
Boredom that turns into anger
Tension that turns into relief

questions.prompt:
Gather round, everyone, and please keep behind the yellow line; the furnace you can feel on your faces is hotter than a summer in the desert, and I would like all of you to leave with your eyebrows. Isn't it marvelous? Look at Mr. Brandt's hands as he turns the pipe. He has done this for thirty-one years, and still he treats every bubble of molten glass as if it were the first. Watch how he blows, just gently, and the orange blob swells like a sunrise in his palm. Notice that he never hurries. Glass cannot be rushed; it punishes impatience with cracks. Now, I am told that some of you were hoping to try this yourselves. I am afraid that is a privilege reserved for people with a decade of training and a very steady nerve. However, in the shop at the end of the tour, you may hold finished pieces, admire the colors, and, if your wallet permits, take one home. Shall we move on? Mind the step; it is steeper than it looks.

Which pair of words best describes the guide's manner?

options.text: Enthusiastic and lightly humorous
Bored and impatient
Stern and humorless
Nervous and apologetic

questions.prompt:
The word was "rhythm." I know it now as I know my own name, but standing under the stage lights, with the judge's pen hovering, my mind turned white and empty like a freshly washed page. I spelled it r-y-t-h and heard the bell. It rang so softly and so finally. I walked off the stage with my face burning, smiling at nobody. For a week afterward I avoided the dictionary the way people avoid a former friend. Then, on a rainy Thursday, my teacher handed me an envelope. Inside was a card signed by every student in the class, and on the front, in huge, wobbly letters, was the word "RHYTHM," spelled perfectly. I laughed so hard I had to sit down. It occurs to me now that the bell did not take anything from me except a trophy I had not yet earned. What I kept was the memory of being laughed with, rather than at, and a spelling I will never again forget.

Which pair of words best describes the tone of the passage?

options.text: Cold and detached
Resentful and defensive
Panicked and urgent
Reflective and warmly amused

questions.prompt:
Dear Members of the Residents' Committee, I am writing, once again, about the bicycles in the shared courtyard. As I mentioned in my letters of March and June, the area beside the main entrance has gradually become a storage space for at least a dozen bicycles, two scooters, and what I believe is a broken stroller. I do not wish to appear unreasonable. I understand that our building lacks a proper bicycle room, and I appreciate that many neighbors depend on their bikes for work. Nonetheless, last Friday my elderly neighbor, carrying shopping, had to step into the road to reach the door. I would be grateful if the committee would, at its next meeting, consider installing racks along the east wall and setting a clear date by which loose items must be removed. I remain, as ever, willing to help with the cost or the labor. Yet I confess that my patience, though considerable, is not without limit. I look forward to your reply and trust that it will not take another three months. Yours faithfully, A. Mensah

Which pair of words best describes the tone of the letter?

options.text: Shy and hesitant
Polite but firm
Playful and relaxed
Rude and insulting

A wake-up call before her exam
A larger room with a view of the city
A room away from the street noise

The student repeated the instructions in his own words to be sure he had understood, and the pharmacist nodded and wrote the times on the box with a marker. After breakfast and after dinner
Only when he feels pain
Before breakfast on an empty stomach

Good communication is not only about speaking well; it also depends on how well we listen. Researchers on conversation often describe "active listening," which means giving full attention to the speaker instead of preparing your own reply. Active listeners show that they care in small ways: they look at the speaker, nod occasionally, and avoid checking their phones. They may also say "I see" or "That sounds difficult" to show that they follow the speaker's feelings. Paying full attention to the speaker rather than planning your answer
Speaking continuously so that the other person stays quiet and listens to you

Yuna was unsure what to say, so she simply said, "Thank you. It smells delicious." This made everyone smile. The father asked about her flight, and she described the long wait in the airport and the movie she watched. By the end of dinner, she felt much more at ease.

She asked for more food than anyone else.
She expressed her appreciation in a natural way.
She had made a funny mistake in her pronunciation of the word.

questions.prompt:
In many English-speaking countries, the usual reply to a compliment is a simple "Thank you." If someone says, "You gave a great presentation," answering "No, it was terrible" may make the speaker feel embarrassed, because it seems to reject their opinion. A better response is, "Thanks, I'm glad you enjoyed it." You may add a short comment, such as "I worked on it all weekend," to continue the conversation. Learners from cultures where modesty is valued sometimes feel it is boastful to accept praise so directly, but a warm thanks is generally considered both polite and humble. It is also friendly to return the compliment when it is sincere, for example, "Your slides looked great too." Remember that these are habits, not strict rules, and customs can differ among families and regions.

What is the main purpose of the passage?

options.text: To list the customs of one country
To explain a common way to respond to praise in English
To teach how to give a good presentation in English class
To argue that modesty is a bad habit

When you work outside the office, you are still handling information that belongs to your employer and its customers. Experts therefore recommend a few simple habits. Use a strong password that is different for every account, and never share it, even with a colleague you trust. Avoid public Wi-Fi when you open private files, because other users on the same network may be able to see your activity. Lock your screen whenever you leave your desk, even at home, and do not discuss confidential matters where visitors can overhear you. Finally, report any suspicious email to your IT team instead of opening the attachment. A single careless click can put thousands of people's data at risk.

My supervisor, Dr. Moon, gave me a simple task: greet each family at the door and help them fill out a form. At first, my voice shook, but by the second week I was talking easily with parents and even making the children laugh.

I also learned that small details matter. A mistake in a patient's birth date, for example, can cause serious confusion later. So I started checking each form twice before handing it in. On my last day, Dr. Moon told me that this habit was the most useful thing I had shown. I did not expect such praise, and it made me think seriously about a career in healthcare.

Proud because Dr. Moon had praised her
Angry because she had to work alone
Bored because the tasks were too easy

questions.prompt:
Doing business with people from other countries can be rewarding, but small cultural differences can cause misunderstanding. In some countries, arriving ten minutes early to a meeting shows respect. In others, the host may expect guests to arrive a little late, and starting exactly on time can feel rushed. Exchanging business cards is also treated differently. In several Asian countries, people offer and receive a card with both hands and read it carefully before putting it away. Writing on it or pushing it into a back pocket may seem impolite.

Experts advise that the best strategy is not to memorize every rule but to stay curious. Ask polite questions, watch how others behave, and be ready to adjust. Showing a sincere interest in other customs usually matters more than getting every detail right.

What is the main message of the passage?

options.text: Business cards are required in every country
Arriving late is always better than being early
Being open to other cultures helps in business
Foreign partners should learn the same rules

Conference calls save time and travel costs, but they can easily go wrong without good manners. First, join a few minutes early and test your microphone so that the meeting can start on time. Keep yourself on mute when you are not speaking, as background noise such as typing or a barking dog can distract everyone.

When you do speak, state your name briefly, particularly in a large group, because participants cannot see each other's body language. Try not to interrupt; if two people begin speaking at once, one of them should politely offer the other the chance to continue. Finally, summarize the key decisions at the end and say who will take each action. A short follow-up email that repeats these points helps to prevent confusion afterward.

Why meetings should always be held in person
Good manners for phone and video meetings

A job interview is not only a test; it is a conversation in which both sides learn about each other. The most successful candidates usually prepare in three ways.

First, they research the organization. Knowing what a company makes, whom it serves, and what it values allows you to connect your own skills with its needs. Second, they practise answering common questions aloud, such as “Tell me about a time you solved a problem.” A good answer gives a brief situation, describes the action you took, and explains the result. Third, they prepare one or two questions of their own, for example about training opportunities.

On the day, arrive ten minutes early, listen carefully, and be honest. Interviewers often remember a sincere answer longer than a perfect one.

Interviewers dislike people who are late
Perfect answers are always the best choice for interviews
Honesty can be more memorable than perfection

questions.prompt:
Every parcel that reaches your door has passed through a chain of steps in a distribution center. When a truck arrives, workers first check the delivery note against the number of boxes to make sure nothing is missing. The goods are then unloaded and scanned, which records their arrival in the computer system.

Next, each parcel is sorted by destination. Large centers use conveyor belts and machines for this task, while smaller ones depend on workers who read the labels. Sorted parcels are placed into containers, which are loaded onto vans according to their route. Finally, drivers scan every parcel again when it leaves the building and when it reaches the customer. This final scan allows the sender to follow the delivery online.

Because mistakes at any stage can delay a parcel, workers are trained to check labels carefully and to report damaged boxes immediately.

What does the passage mainly describe?

options.text: How to become a skilled delivery driver in a short time
Why parcels are often damaged on trucks
The steps a parcel goes through before delivery
The history of conveyor belts in factories

Freelancers are self-employed workers who take on jobs for different clients rather than working for one employer. Writers, designers, translators, and programmers often choose this path because it offers freedom. A freelancer can decide when and where to work, and which projects to accept.

They are also responsible for tasks that an employer would normally handle, such as sending invoices, paying taxes, and finding new clients. questions.prompt:
Last month, the finance manager of a small company received a call from what sounded exactly like her chief executive. The voice asked her to transfer 20,000 dollars to a new supplier at once, and to keep the matter confidential. She complied. Finance managers are usually careless with money
Phone calls are always safer than written messages

questions.prompt:

The Daily Courier ran the headline "Factory Slashes 120 Jobs in Brutal Blow to Town," with a photo of workers leaving through a gate. The Metro Business Wire chose "Factory Invests in Robotics, Creating 40 Skilled Roles." Both stories quoted the same company statement, and neither contained a false number. Comparing several reports is one way to see the frame around a story.

What is the main idea of the passage?

One of the two news sites published false numbers
Factories should not use robots in towns
Different headlines can shape how readers see the same facts

questions.prompt:
Open any social app and you will see posts chosen for you by an algorithm, a set of rules that predicts what you will click, like or share. Because the system learns from your past behavior, it tends to show more of what you already enjoy. This can be convenient: a fan of baking will never have to hunt for recipes. But researchers warn of a side effect sometimes called the "filter bubble," in which people see fewer views that differ from their own. Over time, this may make other opinions seem strange or unreasonable. Some platforms now offer a button to view posts in time order, though few users choose it. Experts suggest following a few accounts you disagree with, so that your feed does not always agree with you.

Why social apps are losing users
How to become a famous baker online
How to delete an account safely

To the editor:

I was disappointed to learn that the Riverside Library will close at 5 p.m. on weekdays from next month. Your article described the decision as a "small adjustment," but for many families it is much more. Students like me rely on the library's quiet rooms and free internet after school, when our homes may be crowded or have no reliable connection. Cutting three evening hours may save the city some money, but it will cost young people a place to study. I urge the council to consider keeping the longer hours at least on two days a week, perhaps with volunteers. A library is not just a building for books; it is a service that treats every resident equally.

Yours sincerely,
Minseo Park

options.text: To complain about a noisy study room
To announce a new volunteer program
To thank the newspaper for its article about the library
To persuade the council to reconsider shorter hours

questions.prompt:
Beginners often believe that a good video depends on expensive equipment, but editing matters far more. Start by watching all your footage and writing down the best moments; most clips contain only a few seconds worth keeping. Next, arrange these moments so that each shot leads naturally to the following one. Cut on action, for example when a person opens a door, since our eyes hardly notice a change at that moment. Keep the audio clear: viewers forgive shaky images much sooner than muffled speech. Finally, add music at a low volume and check the video on a phone as well as a computer. If you can explain the story of your video in one sentence, the edit is probably focused enough.

What is the writer's main message?

options.text: Music is the most important part of a video
Phones are better than professional cameras
Careful editing improves a video more than costly equipment does
Beginners should avoid editing their own footage at the start

The chart was not shared enough times
The colors of the chart are too bright

He attached the wrong photo to the article
He quoted a source who did not exist
He misspelled the name of a union leader

questions.prompt:
Imagine an iceberg floating in the sea. Only a small part is visible above the water, while most of it lies hidden below. Many scholars use this picture to explain culture. These hidden elements shape how people behave, yet members of a culture rarely notice them because they seem natural. Misunderstandings between cultures often begin below the waterline. The English dictionary is full of travelers. The word "safari" arrived from Swahili, where it simply means a journey. "Pajamas" came through languages of South Asia, and "tsunami" was borrowed from Japanese, where it describes a powerful sea wave. Ketchup is thought to have started as a fish sauce in southern China before European sailors carried the idea home and changed the recipe. When a word moves, its meaning often shifts. "Safari" now suggests a trip to see wild animals, a narrower idea than the original. Borrowing is not a sign of weakness in a language; it shows that people have met, traded, and learned from one another. Studying where words come from can therefore be a small history lesson about how cultures have been connected for centuries.

Some stereotypes sound harmless, even positive, such as "people from that country are always polite," yet they are still problematic. They ignore the fact that individuals differ, and they can pressure people to act in a fixed way. Psychologists explain that the brain likes shortcuts, so it quickly sorts new people into categories. The sea below was the colour of slate, and the wind pulled at his coat as if it wanted him to hurry. He did not hurry. the awnings snap open like green wings.
A woman stacks her oranges in pyramids,
each one a small lamp lit for the day.
Fish lie silver on their beds of ice,
their round eyes full of last night's sea.
A boy runs past with bread held high,
a trophy warm against his chest.
The air is thick with mint and smoke
and prices called in a dozen tongues.
Nobody here is standing still;
even the pigeons seem to haggle.
Then comes the bell from the church tower,
and for a moment all the noise
folds down, as if the street itself
were taking one long breath
before it starts to sing again.

Which sense does the line "The air is thick with mint and smoke" appeal to most?

options.text: Hearing
Taste
Touch
Smell

각 보기가 지문의 내용과 맞는지 하나씩 확인하세요.
questions.explanation: Mint and smoke are known by their scent, so the image appeals mainly to the sense of smell.

questions.prompt:
A grey heron lived beside a pond so clear that every pebble on the bottom could be counted. For many years she caught a fish whenever she was hungry, and she was content. Then one summer she grew proud. "Small fish are beneath me," she said, and she refused them. She waited for a large, golden carp instead. Days passed. The small fish swam past her legs and laughed quietly, and still she waited. When the carp finally appeared, it was too quick and too clever, and it slipped away into deep water. By autumn the pond had grown cold, the small fish had hidden in the mud, and the heron stood alone on one thin leg, hungrier than she had ever been. Her pride, it seemed, had been the only meal she had eaten.

Which lesson does this fable teach?

options.text: Being too proud can make us lose what we have.
Autumn is the hardest season for hunting.
Clever animals always win in the end.
Large fish are easier to catch than small ones.

questions.explanation: The heron's pride makes her refuse small fish and end up with nothing, so the moral is about the cost of pride.

questions.prompt:
Dear Mina,

By the time you read this, you will have unpacked your boxes and found out that the dormitory radiator makes a noise like an angry cat. Do not be discouraged. I remember my own first week at university: I ate lunch alone, I got lost twice a day, and I wrote home every night to say I wanted to come back. Mother kept all of those letters, and last month she showed them to me. I laughed until I cried, because the girl who wrote them seemed so far away.

I am not telling you this to make you feel better, though I hope it does. I am telling you because nobody told me. Be patient with yourself, and open your door sometimes. People will knock.

With love,
Joo-won

What is the main purpose of this letter?

options.text: To warn Mina about problems with the dormitory building
To comfort and encourage Mina as she begins a new life
To describe the writer's own university courses in detail
To ask Mina to send news back to the family

SETTING: A small kitchen, late at night. A single lamp is on. HANA sits at the table with a pile of unopened envelopes. HER BROTHER, JIN, enters in his pyjamas.

JIN: (yawning) You are still awake?

HANA: (not looking up) Someone has to pay the bills.

JIN: (sitting down) We could do it together tomorrow.

HANA: (pushing an envelope towards him) You said that last week. And the week before.

(She slides a second envelope across the table. This time, he opens it.)

They give the actors' real names and ages.

questions.prompt:
3 December. Snow fell all night, and when I opened the curtains this morning the garden had vanished. The bench, the apple tree, even the old wheelbarrow had been wrapped in white as carefully as presents. For a few minutes I forgot the cold, forgot the exam on Friday, forgot that my grandfather's chair has been empty since October. I just stood there with my breath making small clouds against the glass.

Then Mum called me for breakfast, and the ordinary day rushed back in. But something small had changed. I think I understood, for the first time, why Grandfather used to say that silence is not the absence of sound but the presence of attention. This morning I was paying attention, and the world was kind enough to reward me.

What is the writer's main experience in this entry?

options.text: A frightening night spent alone in a cold and empty old house
A brief moment of calm and awareness in the snowy garden
A quarrel with a parent over the exam
A long walk to a faraway village

questions.prompt:
I am the last one on the branch,
a small brass coin of summer,
and the wind keeps asking for me
in a voice both rough and kind.
My sisters left in October,
spinning down like paper dancers.
They did not look back at the tree
that had held them through the rain.

Now I hang on, thin and bright,
while the sky turns the colour of ash.
Below, the children kick my sisters
into heaps and shout with joy.
Perhaps that is a kind of ending too:
to be the thing that someone leaps in.
The wind asks again. I loosen my fingers,
and the whole cold world rushes up to meet me.

Who is the speaker of the poem?

options.text: The wind blowing through the garden
A leaf that is still on the branch
The tree that lost its leaves
A child playing in the park

questions.prompt:
People sometimes ask what the use of fiction is. After all, the characters never lived and the events never happened. Yet I would argue that stories are among the most practical tools we own. A good novel lets us stand, for a few hundred pages, inside a mind that is not our own. We feel the shame of a boy who cannot read, or the fear of a woman crossing a border at night, and then we close the book and carry that borrowed feeling back into our own lives. In this way, fiction trains the imagination that kindness depends on. It is true that a story cannot repair a bridge or cure a fever. But a society that has forgotten how to imagine its neighbours will, sooner or later, stop building bridges for them.

Bridges should be built by writers rather than by trained engineers.

Children should never speak to merchants who sell by moonlight.

Unit 7 had tended the rooftop garden for eleven years, but it had never been asked what it thought of tomatoes. When a small boy named Eli posed the question, the robot paused, its sensors whirring.

"I do not eat," it said at last. "I cannot taste. And yet, when the first red fruit appears, my processors run faster than they do for any other event. I do not know whether that is liking. Perhaps you can tell me."

Who should be in charge of the garden?
How long can a robot work without repairs?
Why do tomatoes grow best on roofs in the city?

Thin rain on the roof,
a green hum in the garden.
The earth clears her throat.

Summer
Cicadas shouting,
the road a shimmering sheet.
Even shade is hot.

Autumn
Red leaves on the stream
carry small boats to the sea.
Nobody sends word.

Winter
White fields, black branches.
The kettle starts to whisper.
Someone is coming.

(Four poems, each of three lines. The writer wrote them in a single week while recovering from an illness and looking out of a hospital window, where the only things to see were a plane tree, a bus stop and a strip of sky, so the seasons had to be imagined as much as seen.)

options.text: It explains how to write poems in three lines.
It tells us that the writer is a famous doctor.
It hints that the poems show a patient's hopeful view.
It proves that all four poems are about illness.

questions.prompt:
When the judge said "necessary", Dahye's mouth went dry. She had practised that word a hundred times, but the stage lights were hot and the audience was a dark wall of faces. "N-E-C," she began, and stopped. In the second row her father, who had never learned English properly, held up a card on which he had written one letter: the second S. He had copied it from her notebook the night before.

She could have laughed or cried. Instead she breathed, closed her eyes, and said, "N-E-C-E-S-S-A-R-Y."

The judge nodded. The room exploded in applause. Later, when reporters asked what she had been thinking, Dahye said only, "I was thinking about a card." Only her father understood why he was crying behind his programme.

What is the main idea of the passage?

options.text: Reporters discover a secret about the contest.
A judge makes a serious mistake with a very difficult word.
A father teaches his daughter English at home.
A girl succeeds with the quiet support of her father.

questions.prompt:
SETTING: The deck of a small ferry at dawn. Mist covers the water. OLD MAN LEE leans on the railing. A girl, YUNA, with a heavy rucksack, approaches him.

YUNA: (shyly) Is this the boat to the island?

LEE: (without turning) The only one. Are you running away or coming home?

YUNA: (surprised) Why do you ask?

LEE: Nobody carries a bag that heavy for a holiday. (He finally looks at her, kindly.) I have made this crossing for fifty years. People who run away look at the water. People who go home look at the horizon.

(YUNA turns to the horizon. A pause. The ferry horn sounds.)

YUNA: (softly) Then I suppose I am going home.

(LEE nods and offers her a cup from his flask. The sun begins to rise.)

What can the audience infer from Lee's first question?

options.text: He is worried about the weather.
He wants to take Yuna's heavy bag for the whole crossing.
He can read people's situations from small signs.
He is the ferry's captain.

questions.explanation: He guesses her reason for travelling from her heavy bag, showing experience in reading people.

questions.prompt:
The caravan had been walking since midnight. By noon the dunes rose on every side like a frozen sea, and the sun lay on the travellers' shoulders like a hand that refused to lift. No one spoke. Even the camels, usually so scornful, had lowered their heads and fallen into a steady, swaying silence.

Amira counted her steps to keep her mind from the water that was almost gone. Four hundred, she told herself, and then she would let herself look at the horizon. At four hundred, there was nothing. At eight hundred, nothing. At one thousand, something shimmered, green and impossibly small, and she wondered whether the desert had begun to play tricks.

Behind her, the old guide lifted his head and, for the first time that day, smiled.

options.text: Heavy, hot and exhausting
Cheerful, calm and relaxed
Funny and noisy
Cold and mysterious

questions.prompt:
In her second novel, "The Salt Road", Helena Marsh follows a family of merchants through three generations, and the result is a book of unusual patience. Marsh refuses the easy thrills of her genre. There are no battles, no villains; instead, the tension comes from small decisions made over small meals. When a daughter chooses silence at the dinner table, an entire marriage trembles.

The prose can be demanding. Long, winding sentences sometimes lose the reader, and the middle section moves so slowly that I checked the page count more than once. Yet the final chapters repay every minute. The closing image, a grandmother rubbing salt from her palms onto a child's tongue, is one of the most moving things I have read this year. Not a perfect novel, but a memorable one.

What is the reviewer's overall opinion of the novel?

options.text: Fully positive, without a single word of criticism
Completely negative
Mostly positive, with some reservations
Neutral and without any opinion

questions.prompt:
In the early days of the world, the owl was the proudest bird of the forest, and her feathers shone like polished copper in the sun. All the other birds admired her, and she believed their admiration was her due. One spring, when the king of the birds called a meeting to choose who should guard the sleeping eggs, the owl alone refused to attend. "I do not take orders from creatures who sing so badly," she said.

The king answered her quietly. "Then you shall guard the dark hours, when nobody sings and nobody sees you. Perhaps there you will learn what it is to listen." From that day on, the owl hunted by night. They say that her round eyes grew large in the dark, and that she hears the smallest rustle, because she is still learning to listen.

What problem begins the myth?

options.text: The forest suffers from a long drought.
The owl is too proud to join the others.
The king loses his crown.
The eggs are stolen by a hungry fox from the oak tree.

Madame Orlova's parrot had a talent that no one had asked for: he repeated everything he overheard. For years this was harmless, even charming. Visitors enjoyed hearing him imitate the doorbell, the kettle and the postman's cough.

Then came the dinner party. Madame had invited her richest neighbour, and she spent an hour describing how delighted she was to see him. The parrot, in the corner, listened to every compliment. Later that evening, just as the neighbour was lifting his dessert fork, the bird said in Madame's own voice, "What a bore he is! If only he would go home!"

The silence lasted nearly a minute. Madame turned the colour of her tablecloth. The neighbour, to everyone's surprise, burst out laughing. "At last," he said, "an honest voice in this house." They became the closest of friends, and the parrot was given the best seat at every dinner.

What is the humour in the story based on?

options.text: A servant breaks an expensive plate in the kitchen.
A creature repeats what was meant to be private.
A guest forgets his own name.
A host is late for her own party.

questions.prompt:
Madame Orlova's parrot had a talent that no one had asked for: he repeated everything he overheard. For years this was harmless, even charming. Visitors enjoyed hearing him imitate the doorbell, the kettle and the postman's cough.

Then came the dinner party. Madame had invited her richest neighbour, and she spent an hour describing how delighted she was to see him. The parrot, in the corner, listened to every compliment. Later that evening, just as the neighbour was lifting his dessert fork, the bird said in Madame's own voice, "What a bore he is! If only he would go home!"

The silence lasted nearly a minute. Madame turned the colour of her tablecloth. The neighbour, to everyone's surprise, burst out laughing. "At last," he said, "an honest voice in this house." They became the closest of friends, and the parrot was given the best seat at every dinner.

Why did the neighbour laugh?

He wanted to hide his anger.
He planned to take the bird home.
He valued honesty more than polite flattery.

questions.prompt:
My grandmother, who has lived in three countries, says that there is no true translation of the word "home". In her first language it can mean a house, a village, a smell, even a particular song. In English, she complains, it sounds too much like a place on a map.

I used to think this was an old person's complaint. But last summer, living for six weeks in a flat with strangers, I noticed that I did not call it home until the evening a flatmate left the light on for me. Nothing else had changed: the sink still leaked, the walls were still thin. The word arrived with the light.

I now suspect my grandmother is right. A language gives us labels, but it is people who fill them.

It is a word that old people use too often.
Its meaning depends on feeling more than on place.
It can be translated easily into every other language.

that has not told the time for twenty years,

so that the house will not feel abandoned,

I wind the watch. It does not move.

questions.prompt: "If we let students use phones for one lesson, soon they will never put them down, and school will be pointless." Which fallacy does this use?

questions.explanation: 작은 첫 걸음이 근거 없이 극단적인 결과로 이어진다고 주장하므로 미끄러운 경사면(slippery slope)의 오류예요.

questions.prompt: "Either we build the new highway, or this town will disappear." What is wrong with this reasoning?

options.text: Circular reasoning
Bandwagon
False dilemma
Straw man

questions.explanation: 선택지를 두 가지로만 제시하고 다른 가능성을 무시하므로 거짓 딜레마(false dilemma)예요.

questions.prompt: "Everyone in my class is buying this app, so it must be the best one." Which fallacy is this?

options.text: Bandwagon appeal
Appeal to authority
Slippery slope
Hasty generalization

questions.explanation: 많은 사람이 한다는 이유만으로 옳다고 하는 것은 편승 효과(bandwagon)의 오류예요.

questions.prompt: "Two of my cousins failed their driving tests, so young people are terrible drivers." Which fallacy is this?

options.text: Straw man
Post hoc
Hasty generalization
Argument from authority

보기를 하나씩 문제에 넣어 확인해 보세요.
questions.explanation: 아주 적은 사례로 전체를 단정하므로 성급한 일반화(hasty generalization)예요.

questions.prompt: "Debate is a valuable activity because it is worth doing." Which fallacy is this?

options.text: Hasty generalization
Circular reasoning
Bandwagon

보기를 하나씩 문제에 넣어 확인해 보세요.
questions.explanation: 결론과 같은 말을 이유로 되풀이하므로 순환논증(circular reasoning)이에요.

questions.prompt: "The crime rate dropped after the new mural was painted, so the mural must have reduced crime." Which fallacy is this?

options.text: Straw man
Post hoc
Appeal to authority
Circular reasoning

hints: 문제를 천천히 다시 읽어 보세요.
보기를 하나씩 문제에 넣어 확인해 보세요.
questions.explanation: A 다음에 B가 일어났다는 이유만으로 A가 B의 원인이라고 하는 post hoc(잘못된 인과) 오류예요.

questions.prompt: "A famous singer says this vitamin drink improves memory, so it must work." Which fallacy is this?

options.text: Slippery slope
Ad hominem
Appeal to authority
Hasty generalization

hints: 문제를 천천히 다시 읽어 보세요.

questions.explanation: 기억력에 대한 전문가가 아닌 사람의 말을 근거로 삼으므로 부적절한 권위에의 호소예요.

questions.prompt: A student is about to finish her speech. Which sentence best signals the conclusion?

options.text: To sum up, we have seen two reasons.
By the way, I forgot something else.
For instance, take the case of Seoul.
On the contrary, many people disagree.

hints: 문제를 천천히 다시 읽어 보세요.
보기를 하나씩 문제에 넣어 확인해 보세요.
questions.explanation: "To sum up"은 "요약하자면"이라는 뜻으로 발표의 마무리를 알리는 표현이에요.

questions.prompt: In a formal debate, which reply disagrees most politely with the previous speaker?

options.text: You clearly did not read the report before you started speaking.
That is completely wrong, and I think you know it very well.
I see your point, but the figures do not support it.
Nobody sensible would ever believe a claim like that one.

hints: 문제를 천천히 다시 읽어 보세요.
보기를 하나씩 문제에 넣어 확인해 보세요.
questions.explanation: 상대 의견을 인정한 뒤 근거를 들어 정중하게 반대하는 표현이에요. 나머지는 상대를 비난해요.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is the most suitable opening line for a formal speech at a school assembly?

options.text: Good morning, everyone, and thank you for coming.
Okay so, um, I guess I will just start talking now.
Right, listen up, folks, here we go then, okay?
Hey guys, you ready to hear my big idea now?

hints: 문제를 천천히 다시 읽어 보세요.
보기를 하나씩 문제에 넣어 확인해 보세요.
questions.explanation: 공식적인 자리에서는 인사와 감사로 시작하는 격식 있는 표현이 알맞아요.

questions.prompt: Claim: "School uniforms improve discipline." Which sentence is a rebuttal to this claim?

options.text: Uniforms were first worn in European schools hundreds of years ago.
Uniforms are available in many different colors and sizes.
Most students say that uniforms feel quite comfortable to wear.
Schools with no uniforms report similar discipline.

hints: 문제를 천천히 다시 읽어 보세요.
보기를 하나씩 문제에 넣어 확인해 보세요.
questions.explanation: 반박은 주장에 직접 맞서는 내용이어야 해요. 규율이 비슷하다는 사실은 "교복이 규율을 높인다"는 주장을 약화시켜요.

questions.prompt: "A survey of 2,000 teenagers found that 64% sleep fewer than seven hours." What kind of evidence is this?

options.text: Expert testimony
Hypothetical example
Anecdotal evidence
Statistical evidence

hints: 문제를 천천히 다시 읽어 보세요.
보기를 하나씩 문제에 넣어 확인해 보세요.
questions.explanation: 많은 사람을 조사해 얻은 수치이므로 통계적 근거예요.

questions.prompt: "My neighbor lost ten kilograms on this diet, so it works." Why is this weak evidence?

options.text: It is written in language that is too formal.
It rests on one person's story, not a sample.
It cites too many numbers from different sources.
It quotes a scientific study without a date.

hints: 문제를 천천히 다시 읽어 보세요.
보기를 하나씩 문제에 넣어 확인해 보세요.
questions.explanation: 한 사람의 경험담은 표본이 너무 작아서 일반적인 결론의 근거로 약해요.

questions.prompt: Which thesis statement is best for a five-minute speech on school lunches?

options.text: School lunches are an important part of student life everywhere.
Many people have strong opinions about what is served at lunch.
Lunch is the meal that most students eat in the middle of the day.
Schools should add a vegetarian dish to every menu.

hints: 문제를 천천히 다시 읽어 보세요.
보기를 하나씩 문제에 넣어 확인해 보세요.
questions.explanation: 좋은 주제문은 구체적이고 논쟁할 수 있는 입장을 담아요. 나머지는 너무 막연하거나 사실 설명일 뿐이에요.

questions.prompt: In a claim–evidence–reasoning paragraph, what is the job of the reasoning?

options.text: To list all sources in alphabetical order
To introduce a new topic for the next paragraph
To repeat the claim in different words
To explain why the evidence supports the claim

hints: 문제를 천천히 다시 읽어 보세요.
보기를 하나씩 문제에 넣어 확인해 보세요.
questions.explanation: 추론(reasoning)은 증거가 주장을 왜 뒷받침하는지 연결해 주는 부분이에요.

questions.prompt: In most formal debates, which side has the burden of proof?

options.text: The side that the judges happen to prefer
The side with more speakers
The side that speaks last
The side proposing the motion

hints: 문제를 천천히 다시 읽어 보세요.
보기를 하나씩 문제에 넣어 확인해 보세요.
questions.explanation: 주장을 내놓는 쪽(찬성 측)이 그 주장을 증명할 책임을 져요.

questions.prompt: During cross-examination, what is the main purpose of each question?

To thank the opponent for the excellent speech
To deliver a second full speech to the judges
To ask the audience to vote for your team

hints: 문제를 천천히 다시 읽어 보세요.

questions.explanation: 반대 심문은 질문으로 상대 주장의 약점이나 빈틈을 드러내는 단계예요.

questions.prompt: In a formal debate, the statement that the two teams argue about, such as "This house would ban homework," is called the ___.

options.text: verdict
transcript
motion
rebuttal

hints: 문제를 천천히 다시 읽어 보세요.
보기를 하나씩 문제에 넣어 확인해 보세요.
questions.explanation: 토론의 논제가 되는 진술을 motion이라고 해요.

questions.prompt: Which cross-examination question is a leading question?

hints: 문제를 천천히 다시 읽어 보세요.

questions.explanation: 유도 질문은 원하는 대답을 이미 담고 "맞죠?"라고 확인해요. 나머지는 열린 질문이에요.

options.text: arguably
certainly
obviously
undoubtedly

questions.explanation: arguably(~라고 주장할 수도 있는)는 단정을 피하는 완곡한 표현이고 나머지는 확신을 강하게 나타내요.

questions.prompt: Cars are convenient; ___, they cause serious pollution. Which word fits best?

options.text: for example
however

therefore

questions.explanation: 두 대상을 대조할 때는 "반면에"라는 뜻의 whereas를 써요.

questions.prompt: A slide contains 120 words in tiny print. What is the best advice?

Read every word on the slide aloud to the audience.

questions.prompt: You want to use a sentence from an online article in your presentation. What is the most responsible way?

questions.explanation: 정보 윤리를 지키려면 인용한 글의 저자와 출처를 밝혀야 해요.

questions.prompt: An audience member asks a question you cannot answer. Which response is best?

options.text: Admit you are not sure and offer to find out.
Tell the person that the question is not important.

보기를 하나씩 문제에 넣어 확인해 보세요.
questions.explanation: 모르는 것은 솔직히 인정하고 알아보겠다고 하는 것이 신뢰를 지키는 방법이에요.

questions.prompt: Judges are scoring a debater's argument. Which question matters most?

questions.explanation: 논증의 질은 주장이 관련 있는 근거로 뒷받침되는지에 달려 있어요.

Everything went perfectly, so I do not need to change anything.
The graph confused people, so I will explain its axes first.
I think I spoke for a little longer than I should have.

hints: 문제를 천천히 다시 읽어 보세요.
보기를 하나씩 문제에 넣어 확인해 보세요.
questions.explanation: 구체적인 문제와 개선 방법이 함께 있는 성찰이 가장 도움이 돼요.

questions.prompt: Which sentence about a new park is the most objective?

options.text: The park is a wonderful gift to the city's lucky families.
Only a fool would complain about the park.
The park, which opened in May, covers four hectares.
The park is clearly the best thing the council has ever done.

hints: 문제를 천천히 다시 읽어 보세요.

questions.explanation: 객관적인 문장은 확인 가능한 사실만 담고 평가나 감정 표현을 쓰지 않아요.

questions.prompt: In the debate, Jisoo ___ a strong point about school budgets.

options.text: did
gave
made
took

hints: 문제를 천천히 다시 읽어 보세요.

questions.explanation: "주장·요점을 제기하다"는 make a point로 표현해요.

questions.prompt: If you disagree with a proposal, you can ___ an objection.

options.text: grow
rise
raise
stand

questions.explanation: "이의를 제기하다"는 raise an objection이에요. rise는 목적어를 취하지 않는 자동사예요.

questions.prompt: From these figures, we can ___ the conclusion that prices will fall.

options.text: paint
draw
carve
hold

hints: 문제를 천천히 다시 읽어 보세요.
보기를 하나씩 문제에 넣어 확인해 보세요.
questions.explanation: "결론을 이끌어 내다"는 draw a conclusion이에요.

questions.prompt: In the club, Daniel often plays devil's advocate. What does he do?

options.text: He tells jokes to calm the room.
He argues against an idea to test it.
He always agrees with the loudest speaker.
He refuses to speak in meetings.

보기를 하나씩 문제에 넣어 확인해 보세요.
questions.explanation: devil's advocate는 아이디어를 시험하려고 일부러 반대 입장에서 논쟁하는 사람이에요.

questions.prompt: "You keep moving the goalposts!" Which situation does this complaint describe?

options.text: Someone repeats the same point twice in a row.
Someone raises the required proof after it is met.
Someone arrives at the hall after the debate began.
Someone refuses to give an answer to any question.

questions.explanation: move the goalposts는 조건이 충족되자 기준을 슬그머니 바꾸는 반칙적 논증을 가리켜요.

questions.prompt: Which statement overgeneralizes about teenagers?

options.text: All teenagers are addicted to their phones.
Many teenagers in this survey said they sleep too little.
Some teenagers spend more than five hours a day online.
A number of teenagers prefer reading on paper.

hints: 문제를 천천히 다시 읽어 보세요.
보기를 하나씩 문제에 넣어 확인해 보세요.
questions.explanation: all처럼 예외를 허용하지 않는 말은 근거 없이 일반화한 표현이에요. 나머지는 some, many처럼 범위를 제한해요.

questions.prompt: Which statement can be checked and proved true or false?

options.text: Reading is more fun than sports.
The city library opened in 1998.
The library is the prettiest building in town.
Everyone should visit the library more often.

hints: 문제를 천천히 다시 읽어 보세요.
보기를 하나씩 문제에 넣어 확인해 보세요.
questions.explanation: 개관 연도는 기록으로 확인할 수 있는 사실이고 나머지는 의견이에요.

questions.prompt: Her speech was highly ___, and half the audience changed their minds.

options.text: persuade
persuasion
persuasive
persuasively

hints: 문제를 천천히 다시 읽어 보세요.
보기를 하나씩 문제에 넣어 확인해 보세요.
questions.explanation: be동사 뒤에서 명사 speech를 설명하려면 형용사 persuasive(설득력 있는)가 필요해요.

questions.prompt: Which word names a statement that is assumed to be true at the start of an argument?

options.text: rebuttal
premise
summary
conclusion

hints: 문제를 천천히 다시 읽어 보세요.
보기를 하나씩 문제에 넣어 확인해 보세요.
questions.explanation: premise(전제)는 논증을 시작할 때 참이라고 가정하는 진술이에요.

questions.prompt: The new policy will ___ thousands of workers.

options.text: effects
affection
effect
affect

hints: 문제를 천천히 다시 읽어 보세요.
보기를 하나씩 문제에 넣어 확인해 보세요.
questions.explanation: "~에 영향을 미치다"라는 동사는 affect예요. effect는 주로 명사(영향, 효과)로 써요.

questions.prompt: Which sentence would be too informal for a formal debate?

options.text: Well, that's kinda dumb, honestly.
With respect, the evidence is incomplete.
The proposal has several weaknesses.
I would like to challenge that statistic.

hints: 문제를 천천히 다시 읽어 보세요.
보기를 하나씩 문제에 넣어 확인해 보세요.
questions.explanation: kinda, dumb, honestly 같은 구어체 표현은 공식 토론에 어울리지 않아요.

questions.prompt: In parliamentary debate, what is a "point of information"?

options.text: A final summary of the match read by judges
A printed list of sources given to the audience

questions.prompt:
A graph can be accurate and still mislead. Consider a bar chart showing a company's profits for three years. If the vertical axis starts at 90 instead of zero, a rise from 92 to 96 looks enormous, even though the real increase is only about four percent. Designers sometimes do this accidentally to fit the page, but speakers who want to exaggerate their case can use the same trick deliberately. Another common problem is a missing label: without units or a source, readers cannot tell whether the numbers are millions of dollars or thousands of visitors. A careful audience that asks these questions is much harder to persuade with a flashy picture.

Companies should publish their profits.

questions.prompt:
Many schools now give every student a tablet, and some teachers wonder whether pens and notebooks are becoming obsolete. I believe handwriting still deserves a place in the classroom. When we write by hand, we usually cannot copy every word a teacher says, so we must decide what is important and put it in our own words. That process helps ideas stay in our memory. Of course, typing has clear advantages: it is faster, and it makes editing easy. However, speed is not always the goal of learning. A student who types a whole lecture may end up with a perfect record but little understanding. For this reason, I suggest that schools use both methods, asking students to take notes by hand and to type their final drafts.

To prove that handwriting is actually the quicker method
To admit a point in favor of the opposing view
To explain why tablets are cheaper for most schools

questions.prompt:
People once pictured a library as a quiet room full of shelves and a strict librarian. Today, many libraries look quite different. Alongside books, they lend e-readers, musical instruments, and even garden tools. Some offer free classes in coding or job-interview skills, while others provide meeting rooms where neighbors can discuss local issues. These changes do not mean that books have lost their importance; rather, libraries have expanded their mission from storing information to helping people use it. As a result, a library can serve a retired teacher looking for a novel, a teenager preparing for exams, and a newcomer learning the local language, all under one roof. Critics worry that this broad approach may weaken the focus on reading, but supporters respond that the activities draw new visitors who often end up borrowing books too.

How libraries have widened the services they offer

questions.prompt:
After my grandmother passed away, my mother handed me a small green notebook that I had never seen before. I expected recipes, since Grandma had cooked for half the village, and in a way I was right. But between the lists of ingredients she had written short notes: “Too much salt; Minho laughed.” “Rain today, soup for the neighbors.” I sat on the floor for an hour, reading the sentences that were not really about food at all. They were about people. At first I felt a heavy sadness, but slowly it was replaced by something warmer, as if she were sitting beside me, stirring a pot. That evening I opened the notebook to a blank page and began my own list. My first entry was simple: “Burnt rice. Mom pretended it was delicious.”

options.text: Photographs of neighbors from the village
Letters addressed to the narrator's mother
Instructions for repairing a kitchen pot
Short notes about people and daily moments

Should students be allowed to use their phones during lunch? Supporters say that lunchtime is free time, and checking messages or listening to music helps students relax. The writer fully supports a complete ban on phones throughout the school day.
The writer suggests a compromise that considers both sides.
The writer thinks lunch should be shorter for everyone.

questions.prompt:
In crowded cities, rooftops are usually bare surfaces of concrete or tar that soak up the summer sun. In recent years, however, more buildings have been covered with soil and plants, forming what are known as green roofs. The plants shade the surface beneath them and release water vapor, which cools the surrounding air. In addition, the soil absorbs rainwater, so less of it rushes into the drains during heavy storms. Building owners also benefit, because the layer of plants acts like a blanket, keeping rooms warmer in winter and cooler in summer, which lowers energy bills. Still, green roofs are not without drawbacks. They are heavier than ordinary roofs, so the building must be strong enough to support them, and they need regular care. For these reasons, many experts recommend them for new buildings rather than for old ones.

How is the passage organized?

options.text: Two opinions followed by the writer's complaint
A history of roofs from ancient times to the modern day
Advantages, then drawbacks, then a recommendation
A personal story followed by a list of rules
